#3966. Sudden Illness Sees Miyamoto Miss Nintendo's Financial Briefing, But He's Expected To Make A Quick Recovery

Nintendo legend and creative mastermind Shigeru Miyamoto is almost 74, and while he has taken a step back in recent years, he's still quite active within the Japanese video game company.

We saw him host a pre-recorded Pikmin Direct last week, but he was absent during the Q & A of Nintendo's financial briefing this week. If you are wondering what might be going on, according to a translation of Nintendo's official document, he's been sick and unable to attend.

While this sudden illness has raised some concerns online, there's apparently no need to worry, as he is now in a stable condition and is expected to bounce back and return to work in a few days to a week (via David Gibson).

This follows last month's news, revealing Miyamoto would become the first game developer to receive Japan's prestigious Order of Culture award. This event actually took place earlier this week in Tokyo, but Miyamoto was not in attendance, according to The Japan Times.

Miyamoto's name has most recently featured in the credits of the Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, where he's credited for his work on "original game design". He's also worked closely with Illumination on the Super Mario movies, and has helped co-produce the upcoming live-action Zelda movie, due out next April.

#3965. AMD FSR Upscaling 4.1 Has Officially Arrived For Xbox Series X|S

"We can't wait to see what developers create with it."

A couple of weeks ago, the folks at AMD made headlines when they announced that AMD FSR 4.1 would be coming to Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S in the near future, and the rollout has officially begun today!

As a result of this, developers will have access to a new method of improving visual fidelity (and in some cases boosting performance) in their games across both consoles, which should prove particularly useful when it comes to the lower-powered Xbox Series S.

"Working closely with AMD, the XBOX team has optimized AMD FSR™ Upscaling 4 for XBOX Series X|S, making ML-based upscaling practical on the consoles' RDNA 2-based GPUs. These optimizations enable developers to benefit from improved image quality while balancing GPU performance, helping them deliver better visual experiences on existing XBOX hardware."

"The new Microsoft GDK sample demonstrates how to integrate FSR4 across XBOX Series X|S and Windows using AMD’s FSR SDK. It includes both Full and Lite INT8 models, allowing developers to explore different rendering resolutions and evaluate the tradeoffs between image quality and performance."

Of course, it's still early days right now and we don't have any real-world examples of AMD FSR 4.1 working on XBOX Series X|S just yet, but we assume developers of all kinds will start integrating it into their games going forward.

Not only should this lead to improved experiences in demanding XBOX Series X|S titles, but it should also mean the two consoles remain capable for many years to come, even after Project Helix arrives in the next generation.

@Banjo- Logically, Rockstar will apply it to GTA VI, because it's a very simple feature to implement.

As for your comparison with QSSR, it is currently only supported by two games on PS5: Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei. At this stage, it is mostly a marketing feature with very little real impact for players. In reality, AMD's QSSR is derived from FSR, but in a much more limited form because, as you mentioned, the base PS5 lacks some native hardware features that are available on the Xbox Series consoles.

Furthermore, it is more complex for third-party developers, as it requires genuine porting work. As a result, this technology will likely remain limited to a small number of PlayStation-exclusive titles.

FSR, on the other hand, is a technology that has been deployed much more broadly by game developers, as it is already widely used on PC.

The case of PlayStation's PSSR, which is only available on the PS5 Pro, is different. The PS5 Pro already includes more native hardware capabilities than the base PS5 and is significantly more powerful. Even then, PSSR is also derived from FSR 4, although it still does not match FSR 4 at equivalent hardware performance levels. PSSR has seen greater adoption among developers, but the numbers remain relatively modest in practice. We're talking about roughly 200 games that support PSSR, which is still a small figure compared to the total number of games released each year.

What is certain is that PlayStation's marketing around GTA VI is misleading, or at the very least requires significant nuance. If we're talking about the base PS5, then the claim is false: GTA VI would run better on Xbox Series consoles with FSR 4.1.2. On PS5 Pro, however, GTA VI would likely perform better, which is hardly surprising given that it is a more powerful mid-generation refresh released later and sold at a significantly higher price. However, its price-to-performance ratio remains relatively poor.

Given the relatively small install base of the PS5 Pro compared to the standard PS5, the Xbox Series remains the most obvious value-for-money choice for the majority of players interested in GTA VI.

The claim that GTA VI or other games runs better on PS5 is simply false, on the contrary.

#3964. Battlefield 6 is getting a free trial next week with a decent selection of maps and modes

Battlefield 6's second-ever free trial, and the first in 2026, is upon us.

Battlefield Studios has announced that Battlefield 6 is going free to play for one week next week. Well, a portion of the game is, anyway, as part of a free trial that will include some of the game’s most popular modes and maps.

Though it does not encompass the entirety of the game, the free trial is fairly generous. Here’s what to expect.

For starters, the trial kicks off Tuesday, March 17 and will run until the following Tuesday, March 24. The trial will be accessible from Battlefield Redsec, the already free-to-play portion of the game.

Once downloaded, you’ll find a new Battlefield 6 Free Trial section in the main menu. Because Redsec and Battlefield 6 multiplayer share progression, if you played the former at any point, you’ll be able to pick up from where you left off.

The same is also true the other way around; if this is your first time with Battlefield 6, all your unlocks will carry over to the full version, as well as to Redsec if you decide stick with the free-to-play off-shoot.

Once it kicks off, you’ll find three playlists to choose from. Casual Breakthrough, All-out Warfare, and a third playlist showcasing the new Nightfall game mode and its associated map.

All-out Warfare is what you come to Battlefield for, and that playlist features Conquest, Breakthrough, as well as BF6’s newcomer Escalation - all large-scale, combined arms game modes. They will be playable across four maps. You get to play on two from Season 2: Contaminated, and Hagental Base, one from Season 1: Eastwood, and Mirak Valley from the base game.

Casual Breakthrough is based on a playlist that already exists in the core game, and it’s really designed as a nice on-ramp for new players. It also offers less intense gameplay, perfect for people grinding unlocks.

Casual Breakthrough is limited to just 16 real players (eight per team), with the rest filled up with bots. You earn the same amount of XP in those matches, except when you interact with bots, so killing a bot will net less than a human player. Outside of that, unlocks, Challenges and all other things that don’t depend on stat-tracking can be done within.

In the trial, the Casual Breakthrough playlist includes Hagental Base, Contaminated, and Eastwood.

The most interesting is the third playlist, in part because its content will also be available to owners of the full game for the first time right alongside free-to-play players. Nightfall is a playlist exclusive to the Hagental Base map.

This is a very small map, so the mode selection here is Team Deathmatch, Squad Deathmatch, and Domination. Under Nightfall conditions, lights across the entire map are turned off, so you’re going to have use your NVGs to be able to see. This is also a god opportunity to try out weapon attachments that specifically work under low-light conditions, which typically don’t get much use in multiplayer.

March 17 also marks the launch of the second stage of Battlefield 6’s Season 2, which comes with the aforementioned Nightfall content, as well as a big new update - so the timing works out nicely for everyone.

#3963. The Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Easter Eggs That Did And Did Not Make It Into The 2026 Remake

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo 64 is a game full of Easter Eggs, secrets, and hidden mechanics (did you know if a butterfly lands on your Deku Stick, it summons a fairy?). Now in its second remake, not every secret has made its way forward through the previous iterations, but many have. Below you will learn about a few of the secrets that made the cut, and others that didn’t.

In the courtyard where Link first meets Zelda, there is arguably the most fourth-wall-breaking Easter Egg in the whole game. If you don’t rush to Zelda and instead pause and enter first-person to look around, you will see portraits of other Nintendo characters through the windows, like Mario and Yoshi. In the 3DS remake, the portraits are replaced by an image of a Mario stage.

For the 2026 remake, there are no references to other Nintendo characters. Instead, the tapestry you build over the course of the game is on display. Removing the reference to Nintendo characters outside of the Zelda universe is understandable, but it is a little odd that art representing the full adventure of the game – an adventure that has not yet concluded – is on the wall.

As stated above, the Nintendo character portraits are gone, but there is still a guard you can annoy. If you fire a Deku Seed into the left window, a guard will pop out, yell at you, and then throw a bomb at you. You can’t pick up the bomb. In fact, at this point in the game, you haven’t even seen a bomb.

The Hyrule Castle portrait references to Yoshi and Mario are gone (though Mario and Luigi are still kind of in the game in a way), but Bowser gets a pass for some reason. Both Malon and her dad, Talon, are still wearing Bowser pins on their clothes. And unlike the N64 game where the detail was a little vague, there is no mistaking it here.

Gossip Stones are all over Ocarina of Time and it takes a while to understand what they do. If you hit them with a sword, they tell you the time, and if you play Zelda’s Lullaby near them, they refill your magic. If you do the Happy Mask Salesman’s side quest, interacting with them while wearing the Mask of Truth offers little hints and details about the world. But then there are interactions that are just odd for no reason. Blowing up a bomb near a Gossip Stone still makes it take off like a rocket ship, and using the Megaton Hammer still flattens them for a moment like a Looney Tunes.

And speaking of playing Zelda’s Lullaby for inanimate objects, if you slash a sign to pieces with your sword and regret your words and deeds, you can play the iconic tune to make the signs reform and become readable again.

This detail was exclusive to the 3DS remake of Ocarina of Time, and surprising no one, it has been removed. Ocarina of Time launched in June 2011 and Nintendo released Skyward Sword about five months later in November. For… marketing purposes, I guess, Skyward Sword art could be found in Lonlon Ranch, the Bombchu Shop in Hyrule Castle Town, and the Gerudo Fortress. It was a fun Easter Egg to discover back in 2011, especially since Skyward Sword was still months away, but these days it’s a bit of an odd inclusion.

Though never explicit, the composer ghosts guarding the Sun’s Song (and Link’s first ReDead encounter) have always been assumed to be inspired by Mario and Luigi. They are brothers; Flat is short, squat, and red; Sharp is lanky and green. They still appear in Ocarina of Time this way, which isn't surprising, since they are important characters you must meet to get a very useful song. Fans have also speculated that Talon and Ingo are Mario and Luigi-inspired for similar reasons, but it’s worth noting that they are not brothers.

In the Spirit Temple there is a large statue of a woman and for reasons that have never been explained, Link could attach his hookshot to her breasts. It served no purpose. It didn’t help solve a puzzle. If anything, it was confusing. But we all tried it and there is no shame in admitting it! That was removed for the 3DS remake, and it remains removed in 2026.

This is a very subtle reference to Wind Waker/Breath of the Wild/Tears of the Kingdom and is potentially the only addition to the remake that looks toward the future of the Zelda franchise. Obviously, plenty of characters in Ocarina later appear in Majora’s Mask (another remake of that is hopefully being considered), but it would be inaccurate to call those intentional Easter Eggs.

However, in Kokiri Forest and in the neighboring Lost Woods, the magical debris floating in the air often resembles a Korok as it would later appear in the series. It makes sense, too, because the Koroks are meant to be what the Kokiri transformed into following The Great Flood.

For more on the Ocarina of Time remake, you can find our review here. You can also find our interview with the game's producers here.

#3962. Talking Point: What Are You Playing This Weekend? (7th November)

HYAAH, HUHH, HUP, HYAAH *coughing and splutting* Sorry about that, everyone. Welcome to another edition of What Are You Playing!

Just in case you somehow missed it, it was Zelda week this week as Ocarina of Time finally landed on Switch 2! The ensuing Ask the Developer interviews revealed the game's dev team, Aonuma's reasons for returning to it, Water Temple tweaks and more. There was also a wild midnight launch event in London, Metascore madness, new gameplay footage and more. In short, a lot of Zelda.

That's not all, though. Nintendo's latest financial report gave us updated Switch 2 sales figures, Pokémon Pokopia's next DLC wave got a release date, 'The Elder Scrolls 6' title was finally revealed, and The Pokémon Company continued its mysterious countdown.

Well hey, all that news means it must have been quiet in review land, right? Wrong! We shared our thoughts on Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered (7/10), Marvel's Guardians of the Galaxy: Encore Edition (8/10), Stellar Blade: Complete Edition (7/10), Zero Parades: Director's Cut (8/10), and a little game called Ocarina of Time (9/10).

Phew. We can take a pretty good guess at what most of us will be playing this weekend, but let's have a look, just in case.

Guide Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Walkthrough (Switch 2 Remake): Guide To The Main Quest, Side Quests & Collectables

Feature "I Will Have Been Here For 30 Hours" - London's Midnight Zelda Launch Was Wild

My GOTY backlog grows by the day, with Pragmata, The Séance of Blake Manor, Well Dweller and more all sitting there waiting to be played. But who am I kidding? I didn't attend that midnight launch for nothing.

There's a part of me that wants to speed through the remake to see as many of the changes as possible before the year is up. There's another part that wants nothing more than to take my time with it and play nothing else ever again. Decisions, decisions, eh?

Look, obviously, I’ve got the cart. However, at the time of writing, it’s still sealed for a couple of reasons: 1) I was fortunate enough to play two hours pre-release, so I already know how good it looks and feels and I’m prolonging the excitement; and 2) we’re in the autumn section of Click Clock Wood in a Banjo playthrough and, being so close to the final quiz/battle with Grunty, I want to cap that off before diving into Hyrule with the kids.

GOTY is also approaching and I’m catching up with Requiem and Mixtape, and there’s a dozen other things on the backburner. How long can I resist the call of Kokiri Forest?

*rips the plastic off with teeth Sunday morning and spends all day playing in pyjamas

Hmmmm… I wonder what I’ll be playing this weekend? Surely it couldn’t be Ocarina of Time? Well, yes it will be. I still have some collectables to grab and medals I want to collect in the Zelda Notes app. Once I’ve made more progress in that, I am so tempted to return to my old OoT saves from the GameCube and 3DS games or even dabble with Majora’s Mask!

After going to the midnight launch in London, I left so inspired after chatting with fellow Hylians and like-minded superfans. Either way, the Zelda bug has taken a big ol’ chomp into me.

I will still be unlocking teams, skills and players in Tape to Tape this weekend. I also plan to start Eve’s epic journey in Stellar Blade Complete Edition. Being a huge fan of the series, it is quite unfortunate I failed to notice the release of Earth Defense Force 5 on Switch 2, but thankfully, NL readers recommendations saved the day, and I am once again quite hooked on blasting giant ants and spiders (I haven’t even unlocked any mechs yet!). Looking forward to E.D.F. 6 next year.

My game of the Week is NOT The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Yes, I too will be enjoying this quality remake while fondly remembering how simpler life was 28 years ago, but having one of my favourite GameCube games re-released with a brand new Unreal Engine 5 coat of paint is proving far too enticing. Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is my game of the week, and since there was also a surprise Switch 1 release, everyone should be able to (re)discover the joys of smashing a building into King Ghidorah (and do remember to ask the faeries for Mothra’s help, even if that sounds primitive and unscientific).

I’ve played a hell of a lot of Ocarina of Time recently, so I’m actually keen to play literally anything else. I’ve got my eye on Queen’s Domain: I’ve heard great things about it, and the visual style really speaks to me.

I also recently picked up Alone in the Dark via the PS5’s Black Friday sale, so I’d like to give that a go at some point. Some of the more middling reviews put me off in 2024, but with the cheeky discount, it’s about time I dive in. After jogging around Hyrule for so long, I’m ready for some comforting survival horror.

Those are our plans, but what about yours? Let us know what you'll be slapping in your Switch (2) in the poll below.

Something cool that I noticed is that the controller vibrates when playing the ocarina. The low D is a D, the F is an F, but the A sounds like another D on the controller, and the B sounds like an E and the high D sounds like a G. I guess it can't go very high, as it sounds like it struggles when I try to play anything higher than the high D (controller G). Strangely, it sounds like a B when I hold down on the stick and Z on the low D, but trying it on the A (controller D) sounds like it's partway between C and C#. Because only the top three notes are different, songs like Zelda's Lullaby and Epona's Song sound similar—just in a different key—from the controller, but songs that also use the lower two notes sound very strange, like Saria's Song being F D E. I can't use a tuner as it's too quiet so I might be completely wrong about this, haha... I'm kidding; my ears aren't that bad, I think...

So instead of the Kingdom of Hyrule, I'm in the Kingdom of Corona on Kingdom Hearts 3. Much like every other game in the series this playthrough I'm enjoying this one more than normal, though my opinion of it hasn't completely flipped yet. It's flaws are still evident, but my goodness does it look gorgeous in handheld mode on the Switch 2! And the combat really is fun, if a bit unwieldy and excessive from time to time (a form change, grand magic, the ability to summon a pirate ship to attack people with, AND a combo attack with Donald can, and will, all show up as situational options to annihilate a low level hoard of enemies AT THE SAME TIME. Makes me long for the days when I could just hike up my pants, smack 'em a few times with my keyblade, and call it a day.) All in all I'm having a great time with it, and seeing how well it runs (for the most part) makes me even more confident in my decision to play KH4 on the Switch 2 when it eventually comes out!

I gotta say, I am loving the Increased Class Exp boon. Quicker class mastery allows for early access to class exclusive abilities, which you can then experiment its synergy with other classes and abilities.

Lysander for example is my favorite creation with the most rewarding experience. First, I look at his personal skill, Racing Attack, which grants Avoid +15 when initiating combat. The Speed stat is what determines the Avoid rate, so I checked to see what Advanced Class grants him high Speed growth. Having completed Dietrich's path in Part I, I had access to the Ranger class boosting Lysander's Speed growth rate to 65. With the Ranger class in mind, I invested Lysander in archery while learning abilities that enhanced Avoid rate. I gave him the refined Tempest Bow+1 for passive Avo +10 and +3 when initiating battle, the In Shadow ability for one turn Avo +10 after defeating a foe, Dodge for Avo +5 against magic/bow users, and Regroup for Avo +20 when a foe avoids an attack. I thought Regroup would be useful since Lysander's accuracy averages around 80-90%, but in practice it was hardly ever used in combat nor necessary when foes couldn't counterattack in the first place. I could've given him the Phantom Ring accessory for Avo +5, but I wasn't sure if adding +3 Weight would make it worthwhile. However, the most unexpected bonus is Lysander's secondary exclusive ability, Accelerate, which grants extra speed for every kill. More speed means better avoid rate (and Attack Speed (AS)). As of now, Lysander has an initial Avoid value of 60. Combined with his abilities, he's nearly untouchable when foes struggle to hit him with their average hit rate of 10-30%.

My second favorite experiment is Theodora. She has naturally good growth rates on HP, Strength, and Defense and her personal skill Royal Resolve halves all damages when activated. It would seem natural for her to pursue armored classes, until I realized something about her Blaze Art. Their range. Her second Blaze Art has an attack range of seven. This reminded me of the Ballistician class back in Fire Emblem: Shadow Dragon, with their absurdly long-range attacks but abysmal movement. When I promoted Theodora to an Armored Knight, her low movement made her struggle to get involved in the thick of battle and low Resistance made magic users a threat to her. At first, I reclassed Theodora to the Wing Soldier class to boost her Resistance, but I also thought it would be funny if she could become a flying artillery. Wait. That actually sounds like a good idea. I also realized in battle that Theodora fills the niche of a bulky flying unit. Having completed Cai's path in Part I, I have access to the Dragoon class. I also gave her the Brace ability after mastering the Guardian class beforehand. Finally, as a Dragoon she can move across the map wherever she please. Combining high movement with long range attacks is a thing of beauty. She's basically a flying tank capable of neutralizing hard to reach targets. She could also charge right into enemy ranks after achieving Overblaze status, aggro a crowd of enemies towards her, and then dish out lethal counterattacks which would only boost her defense even more thanks to her Brace ability.

#3961. Honkai: Star Rail Version 4.1 livestream reveals a pared-back, four-week update as HoYo plays catch-up

Honkai: Star Rail will continue the Planarcadia story arc in Version 4.1, as the Star Rail Fest presents a new twist.

A new Honkai: Star Rail Special Program has concluded, which means some fresh news about the game’s upcoming major update. Version 4.1, unveiled today as Unraveled for Daybreak, is the action RPG’s next moment, kicking off on March 25.

Unraveled for Daybreak is the next chapter in the ongoing story of Planarcadia, with the Astra Express Crew now invited to a fan fest inspired by their own past journeys. The aptly named Star Rail Fest is ostensibly hosted to allow more of the citizens of Arcadia to experience the Trailblaze.

As everyone’s eyes is fixated on the grand Star Rail Fest, the Phantasmoon Games continue to be in full swing, as does the war with the Supplicants. Star Rail Fest is, however, the big focus of this update, in case it wasn't obvious.

The event is made up of three large-scale zones, each themed around past excursions of the Astral Express. You’ll get to explore the Belobog Zone, Xianzhou Luofu Zone, and Penacony Zone. Later on, you’ll also be able to visit Pearluxe Tower, the headquarters of Pearluxe Corp.

Each area will feature its own attractions, such as the balloon figures of Supreme Guardian Cocolia and the Destruction Engine, the duel against the Lord Ravager Phantylia at Scalegorge Waterscape, and the Pearluxe Tower’s Alloy King Pom-Pom model.

The hot new arrival is bumbling noirish detective Ashveil whom we've met in Version 4.0, and who becomes a playable character with this update. Ashveil is a 5-Star Lightning-Type character, on the Path of The Hunt. You’ll be able to pull for him throughout 4.1's runtime, which is slightly reduced at four weeks instead of the usual six, in order to rebalance the schedule after the extra-long Version 3.8.

In combat, Ashveil is capable of increasing Crit Damage of all allies. He can also mark an enemy as Bait, which reduces the Defence of all enemies on the field so long as this tag holds. If Ashveil uses his Skill on the baited target, he will deal extra Damage and regain Skill Points for the team.

Ashveil can bully that baited target even further by launching Hounding Pursuit. If any of his teammates attacks the Bait, he can further deliver a follow-up attack that gradually accumulates Gluttony for as long as he’s in combat. Gluttony can later be consumed to boost follow-up attack damage.

If he lands a kill, Ashveil continues to deal damage to the next enemy he attacks. That buff is transferred if that enemy is killed. Even in map exploration, Ashveil can be deadly, capable of inflicting Stunned upon enemies within a specific range.

Returning characters this patch will be Hyacine in the first half, and Boothill in the second half. Once again, due to the reduced runtime, their banner reruns will be slightly shorter than normal, at just two weeks each instead of three — so be sure to take that into account if you're planning on pulling for either of them.

Version 4.1 also adds the Wispae War Saga, a new activity where you can practice your leadership skills by commanding different types of Wispae Soldiers in the Graphia Academy. You can upgrade each one, use spell cards to alter their effects, and later face other champions. You ultimately want to play this to unlock new Wispae Companions, not to mention complete the challenges within.

Finally, Version 4.1 marks the start of a new Arcadian Chronicles phase in the Divergent Universe. You’ll be able to use Waypoint Pass cards to explore the different areas. HoYo is also bringing back Planar Fissure and Garden of Plenty with double rewards. And as ever, if you log in for at least seven days after downloading the new patch, you’ll earn 10 premium banner pulls.

#3960. Nintendo Doesn’t Need To Bring Its Games To Other Platforms, Former President Says

Former Nintendo of America president Doug Bowser says that the company doesn’t currently “feel the need” to bring its games to other consoles.

As it makes clear at pretty much every opportunity, Nintendo marches to the beat of its own drum more than any other company in gaming. It has its own faults, sure, but while PlayStation and Xbox chase trends like live-services and put most of their time and money into trying to push graphics even further, Nintendo is mostly content just making fun games.

Unlike PlayStation with its temporary foray into porting games to PC and Xbox and its controversial, since walked back third-party push, Nintendo notably likes to keep its franchises solely on its own hardware. Even with console exclusives changing so much this console generation, it sounds like Nintendo won't be steering away from that approach any time soon.

As pointed out by My Nintendo News, GamesBeat recently assembled some notable industry veterans to talk about the current state of gaming. One of the members of the panel was none other than former Nintendo of America president Doug Bowser, who shed some light on the company’s approach to releasing its software and games.

We finally got a chance to play The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake and it's still one of the best games ever made.

Bowser said that the conversation about creating consoles and games has always been “different” for Nintendo since both teams work together to “optimise the build” at the “lowest costs”. The former president pointed out that there’s a “huge gap” in the cost of development at Nintendo and every other studio.

That approach is something that has “always worked” for the company, with Bowser adding that it’s focused on creating a “Nintendo universe”. Interestingly, Bowser said that Nintendo doesn’t “feel the need” to “take it beyond the platform”, suggesting that Nintendo simply isn’t interested in bringing its games to other consoles.

The only real outlier to that claim is Nintendo’s mobile outings like Super Mario Run and Animal Crossing: Pocket Camp. As Mario Kart World Tour proved, though, that's not really a long-term focus.

Of course, this isn’t exactly a revelation, as Nintendo has always been known for keeping its exclusives, well, exclusive and being incredibly protective of its IP. Still, with Xbox and PlayStation both experimenting with wider releases, it’s nice to know that one console leader is sticking with its own audience.

We opened 49 packs of the new set, this is what we thought.

#3959. Zenless Zone Zero Version 2.7 brings Angels of Delusion to the battlefield with playable Nangong Yu

Champions Never Fall to the Past indeed, as Zenless Zone Zero prepares for a major update that fans of Angels of Delusion will appreciate.

HoYoverse has delivered another Special Program for the second day running, this time for Zenless Zone Zero. The developer revealed the full details of Version 2.7, subtitled Champions Never Fall to the Past.

This next major update arrives March 24, adding two new Agents, and introducing the Hollow Champion competition.

Most things in Version 2.7 follow on from the Hollow Champion competition, which brings together old friends and familiar faces, as well interesting newcomers. Everyone is in it to win some big rewards and earn glory.

Among the unexpected participants the competition has attracted are the Public Security's Metropolitan Order Division, and even some former Calydon's Sweepers. A big challenge that awaits is Black Wolf Romeul, who’s capable of increasing his Crit Damage Resistance and Interruption Resistance by activating a Corruptive Barrier.

Romeul can also cause enemies to continuously lose HP, but you can beat him by putting together a squad that can deal sustained Anomaly damage, which will break through the barrier quickly.

Our first new arrival in Version 2.7 is Cissia of the Metropolitan Order Division. She is an S-Rank Electric Attack Agent who automatically gains three stacks of Venom when she enters the battle. Each stack deals Electric Damage while also increasing her Crit Rate for a time.

When she runs out of Venom, which will happen, Cissia can generate more stacks by using her EX Special Attack. She can also use her Basic Attack, Serpent's Kiss, to better utilise the new stacks of Venom she generates.

The other new Agent may be the more exciting. Nangong Yu, the captain and lead dancer of the Angels of Delusion, can now be part of your team. Nangong Yu is an S-Rank Ether Stun Agent who can boost her team’s Anomaly Buildup Rate against Stunned enemies.

Being part of an idol group has its perks, because she automatically regenerates Downbeat as time goes on, and even more any time a squad member inflicts an enemy with Anomaly. Nangong Yu can then use Downbeat - after enough has been accumulated - on charged attacks that keep enemies stunned for longer. Her Ultimate triggers Ether Veil: Delusion Reprise, which boosts the entire squad’s Attack.

Returning Agents in Version 2.7 will be Yidhari, the S-Rank Ice Rupture Agent, as well as Seed, the Electric Attack Agent.

Outside of all the very important action in the core story, this chapter also brings new themed events to Lumina Square’s Simmer Hot Pot Restaurant. The Simulated Battle Trial is also getting some love, with updated mechanics and new enemy line-ups.

#3958. The Switch 2 Pro Controller Can Make Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Even Better

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time hit Switch 2 today, and, as Kyle Hilliard pointed out in our review, it is pretty excellent. Along with its remarkable visual upgrade, the new Switch 2 remake of Ocarina of Time adds quality-of-life improvements and modernizes the control scheme. As part of that, Nintendo has added the ability to jump and sprint. While that works well to make the game feel new, I quickly realized it sometimes clashes with another new improvement: a free camera controlled by the right stick. Holding down the sprint button to get through areas as fast as possible can make it tricky to keep the camera where you want it, but thankfully, if you have the Switch 2 Pro Controller, there's an easy fix.

After hours of running around, I was awestruck by the level of detail and updates, but I found myself constantly fighting with the camera, or at the very least, needing to take a strange claw-style grip to be able to direct the camera with the right stick, while holding down the A button to sprint. If you're a casual Switch 2 player, you might not have even noticed the back buttons on the Pro Controller, or you just have no idea what they do. Those buttons can be remapped on a per-game basis and it's a simple process. Everyone has their own preferences, but, for example, for high-mobility shooters, I like remapping one of those to reload and one to jump. I've never felt the need to remap in a Zelda game, but after feeling the need to do so with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2, I might do so going forward.

If you, like me, struggle to comfortably steer the new free camera while running through hallways, towns, dungeons, and, yes, Hyrule Field, you might want to consider remapping your controller. As you can see in the above image, the placement of Jump and Dash on the face buttons can make it difficult to simultaneously control the camera and sprint. This isn't typically a problem in most modern games, as clicking the right stick is often a toggle to sprint, but in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Switch 2, you need to hold the button.

If you have the Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller, copying one button's functionality to the buttons on the back of the controller is simple. All you need to do is hold the Home button on the Switch 2 Pro Controller for a moment until the Switch 2 system menu appears on the right side. Along with Power Options and any Bluetooth audio devices you have available, there is also the option to map GL and GR, the controller's back buttons on the left and right, respectively.

Navigate down the menu to the GL and GR, then select which one you'd like to map. It will ask you which button you want to assign to the one you selected. Everyone can choose whatever makes sense in their own head, but mapping A (Roll and Dash) to GL and X (Jump) to GR made the most sense to me. Now, while I'm using the Switch 2 Pro Controller, I can use my middle finger to hold the GL button to Dash around without removing my thumb from the camera-controlling right stick.

And the best part is that, since you're not removing the functionality of the A or X buttons, you can still use them when it makes sense. For example, A also controls actions like opening up a treasure chest or door, and in my head, that feels like a face-button action, whereas rolling and dashing feel right mapped to the back buttons. The only downside is that, since this functionality is new for Switch 2 Pro Controllers, it isn't available if you're using the Joy-Cons or a Switch 1 Pro Controller. Also, it can make switching over to handheld mode challenging, as you don't have access to the back buttons in that play style.

Even if you don't have the ability to take advantage of this tip, either because you don't own a Switch 2 Pro Controller or because you prefer playing in handheld mode, you should still absolutely play the Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. To learn more about the experience and why it's a must-play, head to our review.

#3956. Heartopia goes to the movies with its next event

Heartopia's Whale Island will soon host a new event that's all about the magic of cinema.

Heartopia’s next in-game event has been announced, and it’s one you may not have seen coming. Developer XD Games revealed Dreamlight Cinematics Festival, an upcoming limited-time event that celebrates cinema and movie-making.

Dreamlight Cinematics kicks off March 21, and will run through May 1, available across the game’s PC and mobile versions.

Dreamlight Cinematics Festival takes place on Whale Island. And, perhaps as an unofficial Oscars tie-in, it’s all about classic Hollywood filmmaking. Not only that, it also celebrates the aesthetics and industrial design of that era.

All around the game’s world, you’ll be able to find festival-themed collectables, which you can then use to unlock free Time-Limited Exhibition Passes.

If you log in during the event’s runtime, you’ll get the Car Cinema furniture set for free. This cosmetic bundle comes with chairs that are modelled after vintage vehicles, as well as poster display stands with unique movie making-themed decorations.

If you’re looking to spend some money, the Deluxe Festival Pack comes with a large Island Sunset Billboard, which you can place outside your home so everyone knows you spent that money. The same pack also comes with the Popcorn Movie Ticket chat bubble skin, and a 10% bonus to Festival Tokens when you sell stuff at the store.

Regardless of which pack you get, you’ll earn collection points for each, which puts you on the path to unlocking outfits like the Dreamlight Cinematics Festival-specific Modern Show Dandy and Modern Show Belle. There’s also a Cinematic Moments building material set launching with this event.

For now, we have the above reveal trailer to go on, which does offer some idea of what it’s going to look like in-game. Until things kick off on the weekend, you best arm yourself with some Heartopia codes.

7 for me. No issue with anyone who gives it a 10 though. For me this is textbook overcooked. Especially in the music. The soundtrack reminds me of that Family Guy bit when Peter wishes for theme music. Not everything has to be a giant bombastic orchestral arrangement. The tasteful chamber of the LA remake did it right.

Same thing with every sword strike having to be so overblown like an explosion. It takes all the weight away when every single hit has to be so epic. That with the music is an unpleasant sensory overload and drags the whole experience down.

And the art style is alright, just weird in spots. I liked Wind Waker, Skyward, Breath of the Wild, the Link's Awakening remake, etc. right away but this style for Ocarina strides way too close to uncanny valley.

But they played to what people enjoy very well and stayed mostly faithful to the source. Like the switch 2 itself, this was a good time for Nintendo to play it safe and conservative and angle to the current trends. People want familiar these days, and everyone seems to like the overblown flourishes.

OoT 2026 is a 10/10 for me. It is an experience, not a game. The tightrope balance of keeping the feeling (cinematic and scope) while still amazing (as in to make someone amazed) the player is being well kept. There are areas of the game that make me viscerally uncomfortable (or elated) even though I know they are there.

This game is what nostalgia truly means. Not some ruined or derided longing for better days, but the ability to have core memories and associations strummed by an evocative experience. This game does this as I find myself giggling or shuddering or laughing or trying not to tear up. At the same time it is FUN. I miss pure adventure games in a world of open world procedurals (BOTW and TOTK managed to avoid this feeling), get gud death runs, and epic rpgs where I need a spreadsheet to keep track of choices made so I get the ending I want. I just want to wander, and perhaps find some new connection.

I’m reminded of why I was so adamant that zelda games were adventure games and not RPGs as a kid (I still feel this way), I don't need to learn combos but attack patterns are engaging enough that I am not playing a QTE, I can wander and discover and while there is a sense of danger, I don’t have to inch my way through, terrified that something is gonna spawn, stab my character and take away my progress. I can smile and be curious about the varied NPCs and make up little thought about their inner lives without having the game having to keep a realistic schedule. Also, oddly enough and I hate to say this, no romance. Just two kids chosen by destiny to stop a big bad in a world of magic. (I know there are shippers in every fandom. I don’t see it, so leave me alone). The presentation is beautiful, the gameplay and control design smooth and with no technical issues It feels like the storytelling quirks of all the Zelda games were neatly layered on to make the characters feel more vibrant, while leading with OoT’s narrative style.

It’s odd. As much as I loved OoT as a kid/adult, I didn’t think it a masterpiece…and felt it was a little bit of a sacred cow, even as I have replayed it many times. Yet this new version with its thrilling music, intuitive UI, engaging but constantly moving narrative style and beautiful but whimsical graphics I now get what people meant by this being a masterpiece instead of a very good game. If BOTW was LoZ (first game) fully realized, then this S2 OoT is OoT fully realized. It feels like a memory, it feels like a reunion, it feels like a link to the future. It is the best way to play OoT. What a time to be a Zelda fan.

I’m looking at the game as a first-time player, even though I am old enough to remember getting it on Xmas morning and playing it so many times over the years. It’s a rewarding experience for a new-comer and also someone like me who is appreciating all the flourish that was breathed into an old game. My god, it’s so good, and it really highlights what made this game so special in the first place. This game and story really captured lightning in a bottle in 1998. When I play it, it’s like a dream. I can already see myself playing it again and again like the original! Nintendo really knocked it out of the park.

Little details I’ve noticed so far: the reactive fog on the ground in some areas is incredible. I think we can now move on from ooh-ing and aww-ing over water physics and now the new standard is ground fog.The other really cool detail I noticed is when picking up dungeon maps, while it’s floating over your head after you pull it out of the chest, the map depicted on the map is actually that current dungeon’s map, and it’s not just some re-used boilerplate sprite each time. They didn’t have to do that but they did and it’s just another small detail showing why Nintendo is the best as what they do.

@Strumpan It’s not the visuals that made the dungeons easier. Nintendo straight up outright made the dungeons easier. The Water Temple for example literally has less keys.

Honestly a 10. I forgot how detailed this game was despite of being a 64 game. It feels really lively. It simply feels like everything has been adjusted to have a more fluid experience and the amount of care and detail that goes into the cutscenes and animation is outstanding. Only real complaint I have is the difficulty. I feel like in streamlining the controls, and with all the quality of life improvements, they’ve made a relatively easy game even easier. This is a jewel among gold standard gaming and should have been treated more carefully, so even if the game if one of the best looking games, has amazing atmosphere, story, areas, its really a core source material that influenced most adventure RPGs today but undermining this game by difficulty that’s like 3/4x easier than previous Zelda games. Its dead easy even with 3 Hearts only! Plus for game collectors, I wanna have a game I wanna play on the cartridge, and cutting out the Master Quest from the physical makes me feel I wont really want to replay this version much and we will rely on future dlc that wont be on the cartridge day one! It was one of my most beloved and most replayed games ever, but gamers grow, learn and handle far more today. This game is made for 6year olds and Nintendo ignored a huge fact, that the first couple weeks after release, mainly core audience and veterans will play this, and this game feels like redesigning would be too much effort for the devs. They could just provide an extra difficulty and still satisfy both worlds, but this completely ignores modern experienced player and focuses on children. I guess Inexoected a little more, but beside the combat the game is 10/10, but combat itself is 6-7/10 anyone else who played it feels the same?

@Dalamar You will have a hard time finding people like that.

I actually think the original is a perfect 10, but also overrated. I played it 2 times in my life and decided that was enough. BotW is way better of a game and other games from that decade fill me with more of a desire to replay.

To me if I am being forced to play one N64 game for the rest of my life I'm not picking OoT and if I'm playing a game for Nostalgia again I am not picking anything from the 64. This game has a spell on people and that's fine but it's not working on me at all.

I just see a busy mess that looks extremely inconsistent over a game that I considered a top 5 all time game... In 1998.

It’s a superb remaster of the quality you’d expect from Nintendo on one of their most beloved games.

Incredible to think it came out 28 years ago and I hope we one day get a new game with the structure of OoT.

@Znake you do realize they have to redesign the temple layouts and other things to make master quest work which would take time reason why they gave us this complete game instead but down the road they will add in master quest in patch form.

THIS is how Zelda should be, more personal, detailed, designed, every character and NPC brimming with personality, great music, story, temples, puzzles, items. And I hope Aonuma, Fujibayashi and the team notice what Zelda once was.

So, for me, getting Zelda back in form deserves an 11.

It’s been more than 10 years since Nintendo released a real Zelda and this game brings a tear to my eyes.

ganon's face looks like it's stretched to 16:9 aspect ratio

I havent played this yet but I have a feeling it's gonna be an 8 for me.

10, and the third game for Switch 2 I would consider a "must play"

Even with the most rosy nostalgia glasses, I really don't understand people rating this more than 8.

It's literally the same 30 year old game with new graphics, terrible aliasing, and a baffling mix of text and voice acting. I gave it 7. A decent remake but nothing else.

Imho, with the near universal praise being heaped upon this remade version of Ocarina, if Nintendo does not make the decision to proceed with an in-house remake of Majora's Mask showing the same careful consideration and reverence towards the original version like they have done with this game, they are simply leaving money on the table.

It takes the original game, works in quality of life improvements and presents it beautifully. The level design of OOT has long been my favourite, and this just enhances it.

Would love to see Master Quest as DLC, but its absence doesn’t detract from the final score for me (the OG OOT didn’t launch with it, either).

I found that TOTK fatigued me — BOTW was spectacular but I honestly like to have my games contained to a reasonable level. This is more the style of Zelda that I’d play again and again.

By far a 10/10 for me. I love the original, but I wouldn't say I had a special Link to it compared to others, I'm only a few months older than Twilight Princess, after all, so no real nostalgia for it. I think this remake fixes all the problems (which were very few) I had with the OG. Shoots up to my top 5 Zelda games, and might replace the original for me. It's insane how good it looks, and how amazing all the presentation is. Such a good game. I'm glad they left the core intact while enhancing the experience.

It's a really good game - 6/10 or maybe even 7/10. Only issue is that's far too easy. I like to be challenged yet I've almost completed the game and have only died the once.

It's a gorgeous remake. If you're a newcomer to the game, I'd call this a 8.5/10 - with the only issue being how weirdly handhold-y it is. I just finished the Zora's Domain area, and holy crap, it is absurd how much the game spells out exactly what to do. First they put a Zora holding a bottle in around the fish area, then they have the signpost in Zora's fountain literally saying "give an offering to Jabu," then a pool of water directly in front of Jabu, perfect for a fish. Any one of these hints would have been enough, but all 3? Overkill. If you have played the game before, I'd score it an 8, since the handhold-y bits wouldn't bother you (you know exactly what to do anyway). It feels a lot like taking a riding a Rollercoaster you've already ridden before. Very enjoyable, but the thrills are milder. I dock an extra half point because I think the devs could have added more stuff to celebrate the re-release (dev commentaries, concept art, old TV commercials, etc.). I also think the soundtrack is mixed weirdly. Certain instruments are way way too loud, and so the atmosphere in some places isn't as strong as it could be.

Just the newly arranged orchestral remix of the OST is a 11/10.The game is a nice bonus lol.

@Durians "It’s not the visuals that made the dungeons easier. Nintendo straight up outright made the dungeons easier"

I can vouch for that 1st hand. Only just done the fire temple but 2 things that stuck out for my like a sore thumb were in jabu jabu, when battling the octopus they have slowed his movement and removed the spikes around the central column and phantom ganondorf whilst in his floating phase no longer fires his unblockable ball (unless i was lucky) Dont get me wrong as I absolutely love OOT but they have definitely made this remake more approachable than the OG.

I only just made it out of Castle Town with Impa, so I can't give a definitive rating, but I think it's really good so far. The visuals and sound are incredible.

Honestly, this is one of those rare perfect games for me. Every change to the original is something that I can get behind, and the game as a whole is genuinely rekindling my love for the series itself. I've been falling out of Zelda this past decade due to the countless Warriors games and the way that the team seems to want to prioritize absolute freedom over all else. To a point where it's outright detrimental to the game design.

Also, it's just nice in general seeing this game get such a massive graphical face-lift like this. It's gotten me to want a Majora's Mask remake that's on the exact same level in terms of visuals, along with story changes that heighten everything.

10/10. I didn't really love the OG for it being too childish at the time. This version finally made me fall in love with the game. I'm 49.

@TrogdorTheBurninator Your average gamer wants an open world game with hundreds of hours of filler content, so yeah it probably wouldn't be a perfect 10/10 if it were on other platforms. Look at how many people are drooling at the mouth for a game like GTA6, which is more than likely just overhyped garbage.

I'm just glad that I get to experience a well done remake of a game with hand-designed content that's intentionally designed. I also don't really get where the "hand-holding" complaint comes from, because the game cuts a lot of the tutorial stuff from the original Ocarina of Time down. Navi doesn't sit and explain how to solve puzzles anymore.

I've only completed the first Dungeon and learnt a handful of songs so it's probably too early to tell but for me, this is feeling like it's going to be an easy 10. Experiencing an all-time classic like this feels truly magical in a way I can't quite compare to any other game I've ever experienced. Maybe that's not the most objective critique but if games are art, then I'm going to let the way it makes me feel serve as my guiding compass for a numerical score.

@VoidofLight If it's not Navi, it's the owl or Impa showing up to tell you where to go next.It's a preference thing, BOTW nailed it imo. I do not want to take away from your 10/10 experience, I'm just a bit surprised so many people find it flawless.

Reached the Zora village and I'd give it a 9.t’s an amazing game, and I’m loving every minute of revisiting it. The sense of adventure is as magical as ever, and the music is incredible (I can easily see the score winning awards).

The graphics are nice and all but since I’ve been switching between Phantom Blade Zero and OoT, the remake feels quite modest visually by comparison, which takes the edge off the “wow” factor. The original was cutting-edge for its time, so part of me keeps wishing for that same jaw-dropping moment. It makes me curious what Nintendo could dream up on even more powerful hardware!

Lost visual impact aside, I agree with the NL review: it plays things on the safe side, but it’s such a charming journey that I don’t mind too much. I’d have loved a sprinkle of BotW/TotK magic in Hyrule Field, and more voiced cutscenes, since the ones included are so beautifully done.

All the comments about the voice acting are sadly confirming one of my biggest worries. I hope Nintendo adds an option to mute spoken dialogue. Until then, I might pass on this. :/

I've seen the Pixies perform "Doolittle," Ween perform "The Mollusk," and Public Enemy perform "It Takes A Nation Of Millions To Hold Us Back."

Legendary acts, but each was kinda predictable tbh. (P.E. was the best by far, but also I was the least familiar with that album at the time. Does anyone see what I'm getting at, here? ✌️)

@Bustacap yeah, I meant DS. Dunno why I put 3DS lol.

I completed the game fully about half an hour ago. I’ve been visiting this site for years but have never made an account, but after playing this felt compelled to.

I’m going straight in to say I gave this game a 10/10 - I can’t quite believe what I’ve just experienced. I have so many emotions, thoughts, feelings coursing through my body and mind, I’m not quite sure I can say anything coherent.

This was my first Zelda game which I played in 2000 when I was 11. It captivated me then and never let go; I have revisited this game at least once per year ever since, including the incredible 3DS version. I was one of those who longed for this remake and to say it delivered and exceeded expectations is an understatement.

When the trailers were first revealed, I wasn’t sure about the character models and the English voice acting (American accents, ugh, I agree with the other poster who said that they just don’t fit this epic/heroic/mythological type stories, whether movies or games). Thankfully, the remake allows you to play with the Japanese voice actors which I changed the game to as soon as I was able (hearing Navi with that preppy American speak I so detest was an instant nope). The voice acting was sublime in Japanese and really drew me into the world.

And what a world! The game is beyond gorgeous, and I found myself smiling so many times throughout; I also gasped, laughed, chuckled and had a little cry at times (I had a big cry during the end!). The original Ocarina of Time was a straight 10 for me, and this is the same game, just remade in 2026. There has been much criticism that it plays too safe, but I wanted Ocarina and that’s what I got. There were just enough changes that some small parts were new and unfamiliar which I found very enjoyable, and I enjoy all the changes. I loved being able to walk into Lake Hylia and Lon Lon Ranch without loading screens, and having night versions of some of the tracks was a cherry on top.

The soundtrack! It is magnificent; I have no other word to describe it. OOT is one of the greatest soundtracks ever created in gaming, and this versions arrangements elevate and enhance what was already stellar.

One of the strongest aspects of the original Ocarina was the atmosphere, and I was overjoyed to discover that this version perfectly portrayed the atmosphere, again in some places enhancing it. It’s strange how often I truly felt that this was the game as I’d always played it, despite knowing that wasn’t true. There will always be room in my life to revisit the N64 and 3DS versions from time to time, but henceforth this is the definitive version (I am slightly baffled that NL reviewer said it isn’t the definitive version, perhaps due to the lack of Master Quest, but as someone who has never played Master Quest beyond Dodongo’s Cavern, it was no loss to me).

I think the reason why Ocarina of Time captivated and stayed with me since the day I started playing it is because it truly does feel like a legend. The archetypal story of good vs evil is done superbly in Ocarina, and no matter which version I’ve played, it always feels epic, heroic and legendary. I’ve seen many reviewers say that perhaps this version isn’t made for “us”, “us” being older gamers who were there from the beginning, however, I don’t agree; this legend belongs to us all, and I hope that when I’m long dead and gone, people will still be telling the legend of the Hero of Time.

1. It feels 3x faster than the original, because it is, 2. coupled with the incredible sound and music,3. upgraded visuals to the nth degree.. 4. And given the magic of the original

All of the above combined and this is the ultimate ocarina of time experience. Speechless...

I finished the game just now, and I just wish the game was handled a bit more.... grand? I think? Like we've already had a 1-to-1 remake with the 3DS version. Obviousy this Switch remake isn't 1-to-1, but it's still really close, and I do wish they had expanded that scope a bit more.

For what it was though.... I still really really enjoyed it, and I absolutely do not regret buying the game. Ocarina of Time is and always will be one of the best video games ever made, and this remake can count itself among that for sure. Just, because it played it a bit too safe, I can only give it a 9 out of 10 for that reason, even if I feel like it's a 10 out of 10 like the original was.

I gave it a 9, because it's a super pretty version of one of the best games ever. I'm not too far in so far, about to start Dodongo Cavern.

It's nice that it brings back that 90's nostalgia and is by far the prettiest Nintendo game ever. Also making me realize more of what the open world Zeldas need to incorporate in the future - a more detailed and narrative experience, and of course dungeons.

Having a great time playing it. But still it is a very safe remake. I would have loooooved if they had made it with the idea of "OoT but if it was made today", rather than basically a 1-to-1 remake. That woulda been a 10 for me.

Heck even if all they did was rebuild the combat and enemy AI from the ground up according to high modern standards to make combat and bosses wayyyy more interesting and more difficult, while also expanding some key areas, for example make Hyrule Field like >5x bigger and fill it with interesting places to explore and things to do so that it would be a whole little mini-world full of adventure, to bring the game closer to what an epic adventure game these days has, that woulda been a 10 for me.

So it's great cuz it's incredibly gorgeous OoT, but loses a bit from the disappointment of sticking exactly to what was cutting edge three decades ago rather than upgrading it (while keeping the same bones) into something that will wow people today. It's a safe and beautiful remake of a legendary game, so deserves a high score, but definitely a significant missed opportunity to do something more with it while they were going to the trouble of remaking the whole game.

Upon further reflection, I think another reason I loved playing this remake so much was because it showcases what I’m desperately missing - condensed, no nonsense, straight to the point gaming. As much as I genuinely adore BotW, Skyrim, the ancient Assassins Creeds, Super Mario Odyssey etc I’m so burned out on almost never ending games with an almost overabundance of things to do. Coming back to Ocarina of Time this weekend I had just finished playing Fenyx Immortals Rising and whilst I thought that another superb open world game, the tightly packed Ocarina felt like a breathe of fresh air and I missed this kind of game more than I’d realised. Perhaps moving forward game developers can come to some sort of middle ground, or even fully embrace the idea that not every game needs to last 50-100 hours plus to be incredible; there is so much room and I believe so much desire for these more contained experiences that have a definitive ending.

@TrogdorTheBurninator The game isn't open world, and that's what you're basically taking issue with. You don't like games that have stories or give you directions on where to go, but that doesn't make the game worse because it shows you into a specific direction- and there's still times where the game doesn't really point you in any direction at all (particularly the Spirit Temple, where you have to basically figure out where to go on your own).

Breath of the Wild wasn't really an amazing experience for me. The game was primarily filler content to pad out play time, and put it on the player to make their own fun rather than giving the player actual meaningful or well designed content to play through. Tears of the Kingdom only further doubled down upon that approach.

@ABmajora With how long console gens are getting these days (fully expect Switch2 to be around for 10 years until the next system) I wouldn't mind 3 Zeldas per gen. The main game as an epic open world masterpiece that always tries to push the bounds of Zelda and gaming in general, a smaller more directed old style of 3D Zelda, and a classic style 2D Zelda. Three Zeldas every 10-12 years, but with each one very different.

Bizarre that everyone was up in arms about Pokémon Firered/leafgreen costing 30$ each but they’re gushing over the Ocarina rehash which costs 85-100$ (plus the cost of the Switch 2).

Also, I assume you're going off of Canadian prices, because the game is 70 USD for a physical copy, and 60 for a Digital copy.

@VoidofLight a rehash is a rehash is a rehash. The amount of new content is what counts, not how shiny the graphics are or how much dev time it ate up. And the Pokémon games were updated too; they added in three new Pokémon and fixed a game-breaking glitch.

@Euler The work put into the game actually does count! Contrary to your beliefs!

Also they did include extra content. They added tons of new cutscenes that flesh out the story, and tons of new music that never existed in the original game. Most of the dungeons and bosses got massively revamped as well.

#3952. All the hype has already made Crimson Desert one of the biggest launches on Steam this year

We're merely days away from the end of the first quarter of 2026, and Crimson Desert has come in clutch to join the list of big sellers.

Crimson Desert, the open-world action RPG off-shoot from Korean MMO Black Desert Online, has officially launched, nearly six years after it was initially revealed. The game has been building up a lot of momentum over the years, which recently coalesced to turn it into one of 2026’s most anticipated titles.

All of it has been leading up to this moment, and the game appears to have landed smoothly, though not without controversy, as has seemingly become part of its MO.

It has not been 24 hours since Crimson Desert launched on PC and consoles, and it’s already become a big hit. On Steam, one of two stores where the game can be purchased (the other being the Epic Games Store), the game shot to the top of the charts.

The action RPG continued to accumulate more and more players on Steam, peaking at a very respectable 239,045 concurrent players (via SteamDB). Though its success was very much expected, we perhaps didn’t predict its peak would be that high.

Indeed, Crimson Desert has been in Steam’s top 100 global sellers list for six weeks, jumping up six spots to become the number one seller this week just before it launched. As we get closer to the weekend, the numbers could climb even higher.

This peak concurrent puts Crimson Desert in the same league as several of the other major releases of the first quarter of 2026. The top spot continues to belong to Slay the Spire 2, which peaked at a staggering 574,638 concurrent players. It happened just days after the juggernaut Resident Evil Requiem achieved its own 344,214 peak concurrent, which was the year’s highest up until Slay the Spire 2’s release. All three are well ahead of Nioh 3’s 88,045 peak concurrent, and Marathon’s nearly identical peak of 88,337.

Crimson Desert has seen something of a mixed reception by critics. James gave it three stars in our review, saying it “lacks the connective sinew to be truly functional,” which is a common criticism shared by other outlets. Many also lamented the sheer number of systems fighting for player attention, its poorly explained mechanics, and counterintuitive controls.

On Steam, at least, players have similarly been divided, with the current Steam user rating sitting at Mixed, based on 8,728 reviews. Unsurprisingly, most of the negative reactions fall on the clunky controls and the game’s tendency to, as one Steam user put it, “so miserably tries to be everything at once, and fails to be anything at all.”

If you’re just getting started in Crimson Desert yourself, or plan to do so soon, we recommend reading these crucial tips to help orient yourself in the game’s vast world. You should also plan your initial skill unlocks by prioritising these skills to spend your Abyss Artifacts first.

#3951. Award-Winning Composer And Musician Jon Batiste Talks Ocarina Of Time's Music And Why 'Guile's Theme' Goes With Everything

Jon Batiste has collaborated with the likes of Alicia Keys, Lenny Kravitz, Prince, Stevie Wonder, Willie Nelson, and many more. He performed the national anthem at Super Bowl LIX. He's headed up the musical efforts of The Late Show with Stephen Colbert. He's taken home more awards than we can realistically list in this article (including eight Grammys, as well as an Academy Award, a BAFTA Award, and a Golden Globe). But as I sit down with Batiste for a brief conversation about video game music, his energy transcends the Zoom call.

Before I can even ask a question, Batiste begins singing to greet me, then nerds out about my NBA Jam and Street Fighter II cabinets. He begins humming the menu music from NBA Jam and reminiscing about all the quarters he pumped into his local Street Fighter cabinet. The Louisiana native and Juilliard School alum has been an ardent gaming enthusiast for nearly three decades, with compositions from games like Sonic the Hedgehog and Final Fantasy VII inspiring his earliest musical endeavors. Spend enough time watching video game music performances on social media, and you'll likely soon find videos of Batiste sitting with famed Final Fantasy composer Nobuo Uematsu, or of Batiste performing gaming music.

With The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time delivering some of the most iconic music of all time (and Batiste famously loving the music), it makes sense that Nintendo would bring him out to New York to serve as a special guest at the launch event for the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake on Switch 2. I sat down with Batiste for a few minutes to chat about his love of video game music, his history with Nintendo, and why "Guile's Theme" from Street Fighter II just goes so well with everything.

Ocarina of Time is easily one of the most important video games ever made, and one of the things that makes it so special is the music. What about Ocarina of Time sticks out to you sonically?First off, if you want to get super inside baseball, technical music nerdery, which I love to do, in the compositions, there's a way that major chords and minor chords in... no sevenths, just root, third, fifth. They alternate, and it creates this magic that is, like, it's wistful, and it's simple. It feels ancient, and it feels like it's the music that is going on in your mind as you're generating thoughts and your imagination is churning. And the major chords are happening just after the minors in this contrary motion that's happening, so it feels like the music is going like this: It's going up – major, minor – like [sings the main Legend of Zelda theme song].

So, it's expanding and contracting, which is a musical allegory for the expansion and the openness of the world that Link is in. It's like [Koji Kondo] figured out how to capture the essence of the gameplay, but also the essence of magic and simplicity, which I think is really what makes... that's the music's power! So, you could listen to the music in the game, and you could also listen to it apart from the game and experience that magic.

Are there any tracks in Ocarina of Time that stand out to you as the most musically sophisticated or compositionally impressive?Oh man. Well, I think of it as a suite, so that's what makes it actually... there's nothing that's more or less complex, but the thought to figure out how to make all of the themes be interrelated yet singular. "Song of Storms" is, like, for me, that's a personal favorite. That's why I like to play it. I like to play a lot of the themes. That's how I grew up! I would play the game, and then, I would go to an instrument. Once we played for hours on Nintendo, we'd go and play Nintendo on piano! It was like a trade-off there, you know? I've been doing this since I was about 11 years old.

Taking it back to that 11-year-old Jon, talk to me a little bit about your history in general.Okay, so my history with Nintendo goes back to the NES. Christmas morning. Duck Hunt. You remember that? Maybe the first game I ever played. No, the first game I ever played was Donkey Kong, and then Duck Hunt, and then Super Mario Bros. Staples! We're talking about the early '90s. We had a room where I would go – it was my domain – and we had this blue shag carpet, and I would sit back there, and I would basically disappear into the carpet playing Nintendo for hours and hours.

And my mind is kind of... my mind can become a spiral; it can become a tornado. And I realized even then that going into this world of the game, even if I didn't win – it's not about winning or losing – it helps to organize the spiral of my mind and give me ideas and inspiration. So then, I started to get into Street Fighter II when I started to play more communally with my sister and my cousins. Yoko Shimomura, who I also had the pleasure of meeting and collaborating with, she composed incredible themes for each character, and that's when I really started to get a true love for fighting games.

And then, we would play so many of the Street Fighter franchise. We would play a lot of Final Fight. There were so many things... there was Double Dragon, then we got Mega Man... all these different series. Mega Man X is [an] all-time favorite. And then, here comes The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and that sort of expands the canon while also blending all of the elements: score, combat, the sort of linear quality of, like, a Donkey Kong or Super Mario World, and expanding the world in that way, expanding the canon in that way. Mind-blowing! So,  that sort of solidified my palate in terms of my favorite type of game.

You mentioned Street Fighter II. There's a meme about "Guile's Theme" and how it goes with everything. What about that composition makes it so it has the ability to enhance whatever video you pair it with?Wow! So, it has momentum in a way that is extremely [sings the melody of "Guile's Theme"] ... It draws you in, which is what you want [with] anything that you're starting when you're commencing a journey or watching something. You want it to draw you in, and that kind of pulls you in as that call and response. But it's an immediate announcement with the brass, and then the bass call and response. So, it's automatically giving you this feeling that something's happening, and I've got to pay attention to it! So that's the first step right there. And the tempo is really... it's a great tempo! It almost has the feeling of the great themes from, like, an '80s protagonist that's in a fighting movie. I think that was kind of the archetype. Yoko was probably drawing from that archetype, right? The action-hero archetype.

#3950. Crimson Desert's first patch aims at fixing controls, but it mostly affects mouse and keyboard

The first post-launch patch for Crimson Desert is here, and the list of changes is promising, even if it doesn't go far enough to address some deeper issues.

Crimson Desert has been out for a few days now, and as positive as its been received by many players, the game suffers from several fundamental issues that anyone who’s played it has called out.

Perhaps the loudest one of those has been how the game controls, which is a problem that stems from the complexity of controls themselves, as well as the underlying animations behind many of the actions the player character performs.

In the first case, at least, something is being done.

Developer Pearl Abyss rolled out patch 1.00.03 for Crimson Desert on Monday. The patch is available now on Steam and PlayStation, with Xbox and the Epic Games Store following “at a later time.”

Today’s update follows a letter to players the developer issued on Saturday. The letter generally acknowledged player feedback, but specifically pointed to complaints about the game’s clunky controls as something of a focus for the team.

The action RPG has actually broken its launch peak concurrent player numbers over the weekend, though only by a few thousands more. Its Steam user review rating has also improved over the same period.

This latest update only includes an initial set of fixes, but Pearl Abyss vowed to keep working on addressing all other points of feedback. A highlight in 1.00.03 is the addition of a Storage at Howling Hill Camp, which can be used to store inventory items.

The most important changes, of course, affect how the game controls on keyboard and mouse. Pearl Abyss included several fixes and altered some of the default presets to make the experience less painful when playing the game with a keyboard and mouse.

There are sadly no changes to controllers, but it is something that the developer said we can expect to see in future patches. More improvements for keyboard and mouse setups are in the works, too.

Beyond the control changes, patch 1.00.03 also includes a set of gameplay tweaks, especially when it comes to enemy health and difficulty. It also makes fast travelling more convenient, and brings a few fixes to NPC dialogue. You can read the full change log on Steam.

If you’re deep in Crimson Desert already, we definitely recommend giving our guides a look. We recently added new pages to help you figure out where to socket your Abyss Gear, how to find Contribution Points - and where to spend them, as well as more generally helpful information like how to expand your inventory, and how to reveal the map.
